questions.q: Why capture the actual execution plan rather than the estimated plan here?
options: Estimated plans only work on Azure SQL Database
Actual plans are always faster to generate than estimated plans
The estimated plan cannot be captured in SSMS at all
The actual plan includes real row counts from this specific run, and estimated-vs-actual divergence is itself a useful clue
questions.explain: The actual plan shows what really happened, including real row counts, which the estimated plan can't show before the query runs.

questions.q: What are the three things to check on a plan, in order?
options: Cost percentage, arrow thickness, operator name
Backup type, restore point, recovery model
Table name, column name, index name
Login name, host name, program name
questions.explain: Cost percentage shows where the optimizer thinks time is going; arrow thickness shows row flow; operator name shows how data was retrieved.

questions.q: What dominant operator does Billing's invoice query's plan show?
options: An Index Seek on dbo.Invoices at 5% of total cost
A Clustered Index Scan on dbo.Invoices at roughly 90% of total cost
No operators at all — the plan is empty
A Hash Match join between dbo.Invoices and dbo.Appointments
questions.explain: The plan shows a Clustered Index Scan reading every row in dbo.Invoices, at roughly 90% of the query's total cost.

questions.q: Why does a Clustered Index Scan reading the whole table match Billing's specific symptom?
options: It runs faster every time the table gets larger
It has nothing to do with table size at all
It only affects one specific patient's invoices and no one else's
Its cost stays roughly constant per patient but grows as the table grows, worsening with more clerks running it concurrently
questions.explain: A full scan costs roughly the same regardless of which patient is looked up, and that cost grows with the table and with concurrent clerks running the same query.

questions.q: What does a thick arrow feeding a Sort operator from a Clustered Index Scan indicate here?
options: The index on PatientID is already working correctly
The Sort operator is free and costs nothing
The query returned zero rows
A large number of rows were read and then mostly thrown away before sorting the small matching set
questions.explain: A thick arrow means many rows flowed into the Sort, even though only a handful actually belonged to the filtered PatientID.
